items.title: Animal Suffering, and Two Kinds of Hungry Ghost

items.zh: 又傍生趣更相殘害，如羸弱者為諸強力之所殺害，由此因緣受種種苦。以不自在，他所驅馳，多被鞭撻，與彼人天為資生具。由此因緣具受種種極重苦惱。
items.en: Further, in the animal destiny, beings prey upon one another, the weak being killed by the strong, and through this cause they undergo a great variety of suffering. Lacking any freedom of their own, driven about by others, frequently beaten, they serve as a resource for the very humans and gods above them. Through this cause, they undergo every kind of extremely grave suffering.

items.zh: 又餓鬼趣略有三種。一者、由外障礙飲食，二者、由內障礙飲食，三者、飲食無有障礙。
items.en: Further, the hungry-ghost destiny comprises, briefly, three kinds: first, those whose food and drink are obstructed from without; second, those whose food and drink are obstructed from within; third, those whose food and drink are unobstructed.

items.zh: 云何由外障礙飲食？謂彼有情、由習上品慳故，生鬼趣中，常與飢渴相應。皮肉血脈皆悉枯槁，猶如火炭，頭髮蓬亂，其面黯黑，脣口乾焦，常以其舌舐略口面。飢渴慞惶，處處馳走。所到泉池，為餘有情手執刀杖及以羂索行列守護，令不得趣。或強趣之，便見其泉變成膿血，自不欲飲。如是等鬼，是名由外障礙飲食。
items.en: What is being obstructed in one's food and drink from without? Those beings who have habituated an extreme degree of stinginess are born into the ghost realm and constantly beset by hunger and thirst. Their skin, flesh, and blood-vessels are all withered, like burnt charcoal; their hair is unkempt, their faces dark, their lips and mouths parched and cracked, and they constantly lick their own mouths and faces with their tongues. Frantic with hunger and thirst, they race about everywhere. Whatever spring or pool they reach is guarded on every side by other beings bearing blades and ropes, who bar them from approaching; or, forcing their way in regardless, they see the water itself turn to pus and blood, and lose all desire to drink it. Ghosts of this kind are called those obstructed in food and drink from without.

items.zh: 云何由內障礙飲食？謂彼有情，口或如針，口或如炬，或復頸癭，其腹寬大。由此因緣，縱得飲食，無他障礙，自然不能若噉若飲。如是等鬼，是名由內障礙飲食。
items.en: What is being obstructed in one's food and drink from within? Those beings whose mouths are like the eye of a needle, or like a blazing torch, or who have a swollen growth at the throat, or an enormously distended belly. Because of this, even when food and drink are obtained, with no external obstruction at all, they are simply, by their own nature, unable to eat or drink it. Ghosts of this kind are called those obstructed in food and drink from within.

items.title: The Third Kind of Hungry Ghost

items.zh: 云何飲食無有障礙？謂有餓鬼，名猛焰鬘。隨所飲噉，皆被燒然。由此因緣，飢渴大苦未甞暫息。
items.en: What is unobstructed food and drink? There is a hungry ghost called Fierce-Flame Garland. Whatever it eats or drinks is instantly consumed by fire. Because of this, the great suffering of hunger and thirst is never, even briefly, at rest.

items.zh: 復有餓鬼，名食糞穢。或有一分食糞飲溺；或有一分唯能飲噉極可厭惡生熟臭穢，縱得香美而不能食。或有一分自割身肉而噉食之，縱得餘食，竟不能噉。如是等鬼，是名飲食無有障礙。
items.en: There is, further, a hungry ghost called Filth-Eater. Some of this kind eat excrement and drink urine; others can only eat and drink what is utterly repugnant, raw or cooked filth, and even when fragrant, delicious food is obtained, they cannot eat it. Some, further, cut off and eat their own flesh; even when other food is obtained, they simply cannot eat it. Ghosts of this kind are called those with unobstructed food and drink.

items.zh: 又人趣中受生有情，多受如是匱乏之苦。所謂俱生飢渴匱乏苦；所欲不果匱乏苦；麁疎飲食匱乏苦；逼切追求攝受等匱乏苦；時節變異，若寒若熱匱乏苦；無有舍宅覆障，所作淋漏匱乏苦；黑闇等障，所作事業皆悉休廢匱乏苦。
items.en: Further, beings reborn in the human destiny, for the most part, undergo just such deprivation as this: the deprivation of hunger and thirst that comes with the body itself; the deprivation of wishes that go unfulfilled; the deprivation of coarse and meager food; the deprivation of being driven to pursue and acquire things; the deprivation brought by the changing seasons, whether cold or hot; the deprivation of having no dwelling to shelter under, so that one is exposed and soaked by rain; and the deprivation, in darkness and the like, of having one's undertakings brought to a halt.

items.title: Ageing, Sickness, and Death — and Why Hell Alone Lacks the Suffering of Death

items.zh: 又受變壞老病死苦。由那落迦中謂死為樂，故於彼趣不立為苦。
items.en: Further, one undergoes the suffering of change, decay, ageing, sickness, and death. Because, in the hells, death itself is regarded as a kind of happiness, this suffering is not established for that destiny.

items.zh: 又天趣中無解支節苦，而有死墮苦。如經中說：有諸天子將欲沒時，五相先現。一、衣無垢染，有垢染現；二、鬘舊不萎，今乃萎顇；三、兩腋汗流；四、身便臭穢；五、天及天子不樂本座。
items.en: Further, in the heavenly destiny there is no suffering of the body's joints coming apart, yet there is the suffering of dying and falling. As the sutra says: when certain sons of the gods are about to perish, five signs appear beforehand. First, their garments, formerly unstained, become stained. Second, their garlands, formerly unwilting, begin to wither. Third, sweat flows from both armpits. Fourth, the body becomes foul-smelling. Fifth, the god, and his fellow gods, no longer take pleasure in their own seats.

items.zh: 時彼天子偃臥林間，所有婇女與餘天子共為遊戲。彼既見已，由此因緣，生大憂苦。復受陵蔑悚慄之苦。所以者何？由有廣大福聚成就及廣大五欲天子生時，所餘薄福諸舊天子見已惶怖。由此因緣，受大憂苦。
items.en: At that time, that god lies reclining in a grove, while the very attendant goddesses who once delighted him now sport instead with other gods. Seeing this, he is overcome with great sorrow and distress. Further, one undergoes the suffering of being scorned and made to tremble. When a god of vast accumulated merit, capable of enjoying the fullest measure of the five sensory pleasures, is born, the remaining gods of lesser merit, upon seeing this, are overcome with dread. Because of this, they undergo great sorrow.

items.zh: 又受斫截破壞、驅擯殘害之苦。所以者何？由天與非天共戰諍時，天與非天互相違拒，即執四仗，所謂金、銀、頗胝、琉璃，共相戰鬪。爾時諸天及與非天，或斷支節，或破其身，或復致死。若傷身斷節，續還如故，若斷其首，即便殞沒。天與非天互有他勝，然天多勝，力勢強故。然其彼二，若為他勝，即退入自宮，己之同類竟不慰問。由此因緣，便懷憂慼。若天得勝，便入非天宮中，為悅其女，起此違諍；若非天得勝，即入天宮，為求四種蘇陀味故，共相戰諍。又諸非天，當知天趣所攝。然由意志多懷詐幻，諂誑多故，不如諸天為淨法器。由此因緣，有時經中說為別趣，實是天類。由不受行諸天法故，說為非天。復有強力天子，纔一發憤，諸劣天子便被驅擯，出其自宮。是故諸天受三種苦。謂死墮苦，陵蔑苦，斫截破壞、殘害驅擯苦。
items.en: Further, one undergoes the suffering of being maimed, destroyed, driven out, and injured, arising when gods and asuras wage war against one another. For this reason, the gods undergo three kinds of suffering: the suffering of dying and falling, the suffering of being scorned, and the suffering of being maimed, destroyed, injured, and driven out.

blocks.text: After the hells, the treatise describes the suffering of the other four destinies: animals, ghosts, humans, and the desire-realm gods. This part is closer to home. The human sufferings it lists are the ordinary difficulties of life, and the gods' sufferings are a mirror of our own anxieties about status and loss.

Animals suffer in two ways: they prey on one another, "the weak being killed by the strong", and they lack freedom, "driven about by others, frequently beaten", serving as a resource for humans and gods.
Ghosts are classified by how their eating is blocked:

items: **Obstructed from without**: they see food and water, but guards with weapons stop them, or the water turns to pus and blood. They are born so "through having habituated an extreme degree of stinginess". Both teachers explain: having the means to relieve another's hardship, yet refusing, and watching others suffer without sympathy.
**Obstructed from within**: "mouths like the eye of a needle, or like a blazing torch", swollen throats, distended bellies; even with food in front of them, they cannot eat.
**Unobstructed**: they can eat, but what they eat burns them, like the ghost "Fierce-Flame Garland", which Venerable Miào Jìng explains as wearing flames around body or mouth as a garland.

blocks.text: The kinds trace a progression in the root fault, stinginess: from the world refusing them, to their own bodies refusing, to food itself turning against them.

Humans suffer seven kinds of deprivation: hunger and thirst "that come with the body" (Venerable Miào Jìng: being born into want); unfulfilled wishes; coarse food; being driven to pursue and to keep what one has acquired; the seasons' cold and heat; lack of shelter from rain; and darkness that halts one's work. Venerable Miào Jìng on keeping: "having gotten it, one must guard it, and that is hard work too."

subs.head: Ageing, sickness, death, and the exception of hell

blocks.text: Humans also undergo change, ageing, sickness, and death. Then a striking sentence: the suffering of death is not established for the hells, "because in the hells death itself is regarded as a kind of happiness". Master Cháng Bǎi: for a hell-being, to die means escape, perhaps to a better destiny, "yet in hell one often cannot die until the karma is spent", as in the Reviving Hell.
Desire-realm gods have no suffering of the joints coming apart, but they have three others:

items: **Dying and falling.** Five signs appear before a god dies: garments become stained, garlands wither, sweat appears at the armpits, the body smells, and the god no longer enjoys its seat. After so long a life of pleasure, the fall is terrible.
**Being scorned** (陵懱). Venerable Miào Jìng: being looked down on, slighted, and bullied. When a god of great merit is born, the older gods of lesser merit "are overcome with dread".
**Being maimed, destroyed, injured, and driven out**, chiefly in the wars with the asuras.

blocks.text: Heaven is not free of envy, fear of loss, or conflict; it is the human world with better furniture. This is the reason the treatise keeps insisting, as the next reading says plainly, that only the uncontaminated realm is happiness without suffering.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what two kinds of suffering do animals undergo?
options: preying on one another (the weak killed by the strong), and lacking freedom — driven, beaten, and used as a resource by humans and gods
quiz.why: "In the animal destiny, beings prey upon one another, the weak being killed by the strong … Lacking any freedom of their own, driven about by others, frequently beaten, they serve as a resource for the very humans and gods above them." The first is predation among themselves; the second, servitude to others.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what are the three kinds of hungry ghost?
options: obstructed from without, obstructed from within, and unobstructed
quiz.why: "First, those whose food and drink are obstructed from without; second, those whose food and drink are obstructed from within; third, those whose food and drink are unobstructed." The criterion is how eating is thwarted. C is a classification found elsewhere, not in this treatise.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what do ghosts obstructed from within look like?
options: their springs are guarded by armed beings
whatever they eat bursts into flame
mouths like needles or torches, a swelling at the throat, a distended belly — even with food and no outside obstruction, they cannot eat or drink
quiz.why: "Mouths like the eye of a needle, or like a blazing torch, or … a swollen growth at the throat, or an enormously distended belly. Because of this, even when food and drink are obtained, with no external obstruction at all, they are simply … unable to eat or drink it." A is the outer obstruction; B and D are kinds of "unobstructed" ghost. Venerable Miào Jìng: the growth "squeezes and blocks the throat."

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT among the seven human deprivations the treatise lists?
options: the changing seasons, cold or hot
quiz.why: The seven: hunger and thirst that come with the body; unfulfilled wishes; coarse food; being driven to pursue and acquire; the seasons' cold and heat; no shelter from rain; and darkness halting one's work. "Meeting with what one hates" is one of the eight sufferings, not among these seven.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, why is the suffering of death not established for the hells?
options: because in the hells, death itself is regarded as a kind of happiness
quiz.why: "Further, one undergoes the suffering of change, decay, ageing, sickness, and death. Because, in the hells, death itself is regarded as a kind of happiness, this suffering is not established for that destiny." Venerable Miào Jìng: for humans and gods death is suffering — though a person in extreme suffering in the human world may feel the same way.

quiz.q: The text quotes a sūtra: five signs appear when a god is about to perish. Which of these is NOT one of them?
options: hair turns white and teeth fall out
the god no longer takes pleasure in his own seat
quiz.why: The five: stained garments, withering garlands, sweat from the armpits, a foul-smelling body, and no pleasure in one's seat. C is human ageing — §46 says gods do not age. Master Cháng Bǎi: heavenly cloth is finer than human silk and never soiled; when it becomes dirty, death is near.

quiz.q: The text concludes that the gods undergo three kinds of suffering. What are they, and how does the translation render them?
options: dying and falling; being scorned; being maimed, destroyed, injured, and driven out
quiz.why: "For this reason, the gods undergo three kinds of suffering: the suffering of dying and falling, the suffering of being scorned, and the suffering of being maimed, destroyed, injured, and driven out." The third arises from war with the asuras. Note that the Chinese itself orders the third's four terms differently in its two mentions, and the translation follows each. (The passage describing the war, its four kinds of weapons, and its causes is not translated in the Ru-Yi version; logged in the correction list.)
